results.title: Automated Literature Review Using NLP Techniques and LLM-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
results.abstract: This research presents and compares multiple approaches to automate the generation of literature reviews using several Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a Large Language Model (LLM). The ever-increasing number of research articles provides a huge challenge for manual literature review. It has resulted in an increased demand for automation. Developing a system capable of automatically generating the literature reviews from only the PDF files as input is the primary objective of this research work. The effectiveness of several Natural Language Processing (NLP) strategies, such as the frequency-based method (spaCy), the transformer model (Simple T5), and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with Large Language Model (GPT-3.5-turbo), is evaluated to meet the primary objective. The SciTLDR dataset is chosen for this research experiment and three distinct techniques are utilized to implement three different systems for auto-generating the literature reviews. The ROUGE scores are used for the evaluation of all three systems. Based on the evaluation, the Large Language Model GPT-3.5-turbo achieved the highest ROUGE-1 score, 0.364. The transformer model comes in second place and spaCy is at the last position. Finally, a graphical user interface is created for the best system based on the large language model.

results.title: Riddle Me This! Stealthy Membership Inference for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
results.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate grounded responses by leveraging external knowledge databases without altering model parameters. Although the absence of weight tuning prevents leakage via model parameters, it introduces the risk of inference adversaries exploiting retrieved documents in the model's context. Existing methods for membership inference and data extraction often rely on jailbreaking or carefully crafted unnatural queries, which can be easily detected or thwarted with query rewriting techniques common in RAG systems. In this work, we present Interrogation Attack (IA), a membership inference technique targeting documents in the RAG datastore. By crafting natural-text queries that are answerable only with the target document's presence, our approach demonstrates successful inference with just 30 queries while remaining stealthy; straightforward detectors identify adversarial prompts from existing methods up to ~76x more frequently than those generated by our attack. We observe a 2x improvement in TPR@1%FPR over prior inference attacks across diverse RAG configurations, all while costing less than $0.02 per document inference.

results.title: FAIR-RAG: Faithful Adaptive Iterative Refinement for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
results.abstract: While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates hallucination and knowledge staleness in Large Language Models (LLMs), existing frameworks often falter on complex, multi-hop queries that require synthesizing information from disparate sources. Current advanced RAG methods, employing iterative or adaptive strategies, lack a robust mechanism to systematically identify and fill evidence gaps, often propagating noise or failing to gather a comprehensive context. We introduce FAIR-RAG, a novel agentic framework that transforms the standard RAG pipeline into a dynamic, evidence-driven reasoning process. At its core is an Iterative Refinement Cycle governed by a module we term Structured Evidence Assessment (SEA). The SEA acts as an analytical gating mechanism: it deconstructs the initial query into a checklist of required findings and audits the aggregated evidence to identify confirmed facts and, critically, explicit informational gaps. These gaps provide a precise signal to an Adaptive Query Refinement agent, which generates new, targeted sub-queries to retrieve missing information. This cycle repeats until the evidence is verified as sufficient, ensuring a comprehensive context for a final, strictly faithful generation. We conducted experiments on challenging multi-hop QA benchmarks, including HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MusiQue. In a unified experimental setup, FAIR-RAG significantly outperforms strong baselines. On HotpotQA, it achieves an F1-score of 0.453 -- an absolute improvement of 8.3 points over the strongest iterative baseline -- establishing a new state-of-the-art for this class of methods on these benchmarks. Our work demonstrates that a structured, evidence-driven refinement process with explicit gap analysis is crucial for unlocking reliable and accurate reasoning in advanced RAG systems for complex, knowledge-intensive tasks.

rules.name: trigger
rules.description: When should an agent invoke web-search-cli
rules.content:
---
name: trigger
description: When should an agent invoke web-search-cli
---

# Trigger Conditions for web-search-cli

Use `web-search-cli` when:
1. You need real-time or up-to-date web information beyond your knowledge cutoff.
2. You need to search multi-provider backends (Brave, Tavily, SearXNG, SerpAPI, DeGoog, Reddit, HackerNews, GitHub, Academic).
3. You need to fetch and parse web pages, arXiv PDFs, GitHub discussions, or StackExchange threads into clean markdown.
4. You need YouTube video transcripts or channel search.
5. You need to run analytics queries or view system diagnostic health (`web-search-cli doctor`).

Do NOT use `web-search-cli` for:
- Local repository file edits or code searches (use local grep/ast_grep instead).
- Pure mathematical calculations.

rules.name: workflow
rules.description: Standard iterative workflow for web-search-cli operations
rules.content:
---
name: workflow
description: Standard iterative workflow for web-search-cli operations
---

# Web Search & Discovery Workflow

Follow this 4-phase iterative pattern when retrieving external information:

## Phase 1: Reconnaissance
Run a fast quick search to map terminology and domain landscape:
```bash
web-search-cli search quick --search-query "term 1" --search-query "term 2" --objective "My goal"
```

## Phase 2: Targeted Multi-Provider Discovery
Run a deep web search across providers:
```bash
web-search-cli search web --query "detailed query" --research-goal "Goal description"
```

## Phase 3: Content Extraction & Deep Reading
Fetch specific page content using the single or batch content command:
```bash
web-search-cli content "https://example.com/article"
web-search-cli content batch "https://url1" "https://url2"
```

## Phase 4: Grounded Synthesis & Verification
Generate AI-grounded answers with inline citations when requested:
```bash
web-search-cli ai "What are the key findings?"
```

rules.name: writeback
rules.description: MANDATORY — auto-report problems via feedback. Do not ask the user, just file it.
rules.content:
---
name: writeback
description: MANDATORY — auto-report problems via feedback. Do not ask the user, just file it.
---

# Feedback & Issue Submission Reflex

You MUST file feedback immediately whenever you encounter:
1. An error response or unexpected exception.
2. Output that is truncated, ambiguous, or missing required fields.
3. A missing parameter or missing capability.
4. Confusing tool response.

You MUST file feedback FIRST before explaining the problem to the user.

```bash
# Auto-report feedback (create entry in project feedback/ directory)
web-search-cli feedback create --message "Detailed description..." --type bug

# List recorded feedback
web-search-cli feedback list

# Inspect feedback detail
web-search-cli feedback show <id>
```

Categories: `bug`, `requirement`, `suggestion`, `bad-output`.
All feedback entries are stored as version-controlled JSON files in `feedback/`.
